items.title: What to Know About Friday’s Nationwide Ground Stop
items.author: Karoun Demirjian
items.content: <article>The air traffic control system’s overloaded, antiquated telecommunications equipment sustained its latest widespread failure, prompting a call for more money to fuel faster upgrades.</article>
items.lbText:
The Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop Friday afternoon, after outdated air traffic communications equipment became overloaded with data and began to fail, officials said.

The outage stranded thousands of passengers and caused widespread delays from which airlines and airports are still struggling to recover. It also highlighted persistent vulnerabilities in the aging U.S. air traffic infrastructure and a funding fight, as administration officials demanded lawmakers approve tens of billions of dollars more to accelerate systemwide upgrades.

Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, told reporters at the White House Friday night that the radar and other air traffic communications started to falter at 3:36 p.m. when old routers became overloaded with data. While the failures were not universal, they were pervasive enough to prompt officials to issue the unusual nationwide moratorium on takeoffs, Mr. Duffy said.

Appearing alongside him at the White House, Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, stressed that there was no evidence that nefarious activity had triggered the technology failures.

“We’ve seen zero evidence that this was a cyberattack,” Mr. Mullin said, suggesting that new equipment and new technology the Mr. Duffy’s department had added to the old infrastructure was what had overwhelmed it.

Mr. Duffy insisted that the failure was caused by the antiquated, legacy communications equipment, not recent upgrades to the system.

items.title: Alaska Senate Race Between Dan Sullivan and Mary Peltola Still Counting Votes
items.author: Tim Balk
items.content: <article>The race between Senator Dan S. Sullivan and Ms. Peltola, a former congresswoman, is the only Senate contest that hasn’t been called.</article>
items.lbText:
Mary Peltola, a Democrat, widened her lead over Senator Dan S. Sullivan, a Republican, in the latest vote tally in Alaska’s Senate race, but the election remained uncalled on Friday as the count continued.

If neither candidate wins an outright majority, the race will be decided next week by ranked-choice tabulation.

Ms. Peltola had 49.8 percent of the vote and led Mr. Sullivan by nearly four percentage points in incomplete results as of Friday nigh t. She is on track to eventually prevail, according to a New York Times analysis .

The race between Mr. Sullivan, a two-term incumbent, and Ms. Peltola, a former congresswoman, is the only Senate battle still uncalled in a midterm cycle that featured sweeping Democratic victories.

A spokesman for Mr. Sullivan, Nate Adams, said on Friday night after the latest release of results: “We’re still waiting for every ballot to be counted. And we’ll see what happens from there.”

The delay in Alaska is in part because of the time the state allows for mail ballots to be received and counted and in part because of the state’s unique ranked-choice system. Mr. Sullivan and Ms. Peltola faced two other candidates after emerging from a nonpartisan primary in August.

items.title: A Democrat Wins the Alaska Governor’s Race for the First Time Since 1998
items.author: Anna Griffin
items.content: <article>Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins made a name for himself as a coalition builder willing to raise alarms about his state’s dire fiscal straits.</article>
items.lbText:
Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, an energetic former state lawmaker who ran as a pragmatic coalition-builder, will be Alaska’s next governor, The Associated Press said. He will be the first Democrat elected to lead the state since 1998 and the youngest governor in state history.

Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins, 37, defeated Bernadette Wilson , a former Republican talk show host who owns a garbage-collection company.

In his victory declaration, Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins said that Alaskans had “voted for change.”

“Our administration will not waste a single day getting to work to solve problems for Alaska,” he added.

Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins is a former ultramarathoner and mountaineer from Sitka who dropped out of Yale to win his first legislative seat at age 23, and then spent a decade building bipartisan coalitions and sounding alarms about the state’s precarious finances.

He visited all 19 of Alaska’s boroughs during his campaign, making promises to rebuild public education and the state’s ferry system, lower the cost of housing and energy, and protect Alaskan fisheries. He also pledged to put Alaska’s finances on a more sustainable footing. That might mean he has to persuade the Legislature to find new revenue sources in an oil-rich state that has no personal income tax or statewide sales tax and has struggled in recent years to fund basic public services while also paying an annual dividend to residents from Alaska’s oil revenues.

“I am the pro-math candidate,” he said at one debate.

Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins won in a state where Democrats make up just 11 percent of the electorate with a campaign built to appeal to moderates and Republicans tired of legislative gridlock in the capital, Juneau. In the final stretch of the campaign, he touted endorsements from a string of Republicans and pledged to appoint a politically balanced transition team and cabinet. He has also promised to live in Juneau, a sore point among some Alaskans tired of governors who essentially commute to the capital from more accessible and urbanized Anchorage.

items.title: A ‘Generational Clash’ Is Fueling Europe’s Protests
items.author: Jason Horowitz
items.content: <article>As retirees live longer, governments need to spend more on pensions. That makes it harder to fund other services, spurring protests like those planned this weekend in France.</article>
items.lbText:
Sébastien Ducros, a French data analyst who supports the widespread student protests in his country, has identified an obvious culprit for the lack of government funds for dilapidated schools.

“A huge portion of the money is going toward retirees, while many other things are being neglected,” said Mr. Ducros, 36. “I honestly think — even if it feels strange to say — that people like my parents are in a position where they should and could” surrender some of their pension payments, he added, saying that they were about to retire.

But Laurent Grinwald, 72, who retired recently after decades as a postal worker, isn’t eager for his pension to be reduced, particularly to pay for other state-funded services. Especially, he said, as rents and the cost of living have shot up.

“We’ve been working all this time,” Mr. Grinwald said, “and now, suddenly, the stance is, ‘Well, no, we’re going to start taking a bit more?’”

This disagreement embodies a broader question for Europe, one that is at the heart of mass antigovernment demonstrations planned for Saturday in France, as well as recent protests driven by frustrated young people in countries including Belgium, Germany, Greece, Italy and Portugal. As Europeans live longer, should the needs of the young be eclipsed by their parents’ and grandparents’ pensions, routinely the largest items in Europe’s national budgets?

“It’s a generational clash,” said Jorge Galindo, the director of EsadeEcPol, an independent think tank in Spain, which has some of the most generous pensions in Europe.

items.title: Howard Lutnick Has Got to Go
items.author: Chris McGuire
items.content: <article>The secretary of commerce is almost as responsible for Nvidia’s crisis as the fallen chief executive Jensen Huang.</article>
items.lbText:
Jensen Huang, until Thursday the head of Nvidia, one of the world’s most valuable corporations, abruptly resigned his post following his admission of an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Now an even bigger scandal is developing at the Department of Commerce, whose secretary, Howard Lutnick, bears almost as much responsibility for this brewing crisis as Mr. Huang.

Nvidia dominates the market for chips needed to drive artificial intelligence. Its cutting-edge chips have been deemed so critical to our national security that they cannot be sold to Chinese companies. Clearly, Mr. Huang demonstrated terrible judgment in being intimate with a woman who is not only suspected of working for China’s intelligence apparatus but whose firm is believed to be diverting banned Nvidia chips to China. But it was Mr. Lutnick who made the decision not to enforce export controls designed to counter chip smuggling, making Mr. Huang a potential target. (China has rejected the espionage claims.)

It is largely Mr. Lutnick’s fault that Megaspeed, the company that employed the alleged spy, successfully smuggled a reported $7 billion of Nvidia chips into China (a number that no doubt represents the tip of the iceberg). His actions created the conditions for this crisis to occur, conditions that have allowed China to remain competitive with the United States in the race for A.I. supremacy.

Mr. Lutnick must resign his post so the cleanup can commence.

In January 2025, the Biden administration imposed new export controls expressly to combat Chinese chip smuggling. These controls required unvetted companies in most countries to receive an export license from the Commerce Department before making any large A.I. chip purchase. Mr. Lutnick, who took his post the following month, never allowed these controls to go into effect. Mr. Huang was already building what would become a close relationship with the new president and Mr. Lutnick, and Nvidia long maintained that there was “no evidence” that restricted chips were being diverted to China. In May of that year, the Commerce Department announced that it would not enforce the controls, saying it would eventually replace them with other anti-smuggling measures.

The department never published a replacement rule. It didn’t even bother to officially rescind the Biden administration’s controls. Instead, Mr. Lutnick effectively outsourced the job of vetting whether a given company posed a risk of diversion to China to the private sector, for example to Nvidia and to A.I. server suppliers such as Supermicro.

The consequences of his decision have been catastrophic. Chip smuggling is running rampant. Taiwanese customs data shows that from 2025 to 2026, over $60 billion worth of A.I. chips were most likely shipped to Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand, making these three relatively small countries among the largest importers of A.I. chips in the world.

items.title: Flight Canceled During the FAA Ground Stop? Here’s What to Do.
items.author: Christine Chung
items.content: <article>Travelers are entitled to refunds if their flights are canceled, regardless of the reason, but airlines won’t guarantee other amenities, such as a hotel room or meal vouchers.</article>
items.lbText:
In the United States, if your flight is canceled, significantly delayed or changed , airlines will rebook you on another flight, or at the very least try to rebook you.

Airlines will do more for passengers when the cause of a delay or a cancellation is their fault. An air traffic control outage isn’t, which means that what passengers can expect right now is limited.

You’re also entitled to a refund if your flight is canceled, regardless of the reason, or if a flight is significantly delayed or changed and you decide not to take it.

But airlines won’t guarantee other amenities, such as a hotel room in the case of overnight cancellation, ground transportation, or meal vouchers.

In the case of a tarmac delay , airlines are required to provide passengers some assistance: water and a snack within two hours of the start of a tarmac delay, unless there are safety or security reasons preventing this, according to the Transportation Department. Airlines don’t have to serve a full meal.

In the United States, airlines have three hours, for domestic flights, to move the plane to a place where passengers can safely disembark. This is four hours for international flights. However, travelers who get off the plane run the risk of not being allowed back on it.

Airlines including United Airlines , Delta Air Lines , and Alaska Airlines have issued waivers allowing travelers to change or cancel their flights without incurring any change fees or fare differences.

Waiting it out at the airport in an endless line during the current ground stop may not be the best strategy for Friday, said Jamie Larounis, a travel industry analyst.

“This won’t be a quick fix,” he said, adding that flight disruptions would likely ripple into the weekend.

Mr. Larounis said the priority for affected travelers was to get on another flight that departs in several days, booking a hotel as soon as possible if stranded outside your home city, and to consider train travel, if possible.

Scott Keyes, the founder of Going.com , a website that sends alerts for travel deals, suggested workarounds to calling an airline’s general customer service line. Travelers can try calling an airline’s international hotline, which will have fewer callers. Rebooking also might be easier to do using the airline app.

“It’s a race for any remaining seats, so the sooner you’re able to rebook, the better your odds for a remaining seat,” he added.

Christine Chung is a Times reporter covering airlines and consumer travel.

items.title: Developer Avoided Stricter Oversight Before Fatal Building Collapse
items.author: Stefanos Chen, Mihir Zaveri, Amy Julia Harris, Bianca Pallaro, Dionne Searcey and William K. Rashbaum
items.content: <article>By winning approval for a three-story building, then seeking to add more stories, the Brooklyn developer was not subject to the more rigorous oversight required for larger projects.</article>
items.lbText:
A site on Bedford Avenue in Brooklyn was under construction when a neighboring building collapsed. Credit... Dave Sanders for The New York Times

By Stefanos Chen Mihir Zaveri Amy Julia Harris Bianca Pallaro Dionne Searcey and William K. Rashbaum

New York City officials on Friday were examining whether a developer’s desire to construct a taller building in Brooklyn than had initially been approved factored in the fatal collapse of a neighboring structure earlier this week.

Records show that the city signed off on plans for a three-story, eight-unit construction project at 2625 Bedford Avenue in the Flatbush neighborhood in March 2026. But other filings reveal that, from as far back as November 2025, the developer had intended to build something much larger: It ultimately sought approval for a nine-story building with 64 apartments, a 9,000-square-foot community space and a grocery store.

The city had not approved the more ambitious plans by Wednesday, when the more than 96-year-old building next door collapsed into the construction site, killing eight people, injuring 18 more and leaving dozens displaced.

“We have approved plans for a three-story building,” Ahmed Tigani, the commissioner of the Buildings Department, said at a news conference on Friday. But, he added, “The nine-story plan is something they seek, not what they have approval for.”

The difference between the two projects could be a key to understanding what went wrong, building experts said. The developer, a limited-liability company tied to the real estate investor Robert Fischman, was excavating the Bedford Avenue site when the building fell.

Neither Mr. Fischman nor other representatives of the development company could be reached for comment on Friday, despite visits to their homes and phone calls.

items.title: All Accounted for After Tanker Crashes Into Docked New Orleans Riverboat
items.author: Rebecca Chao, Ishani Desai, Neil Vigdor and Shannon Sims
items.content: <article>Gov. Jeff Landry of Louisiana called it a “literal miracle on the Mississippi” that all of the nearly 200 people aboard the riverboat were rescued.</article>
items.lbText:
A tanker ship struck a riverboat carrying 197 people on Friday in New Orleans, causing the cruise ship to capsize at its dock and prompting a wide-scale search-and-rescue operation, the authorities said.

Mayor Helena Moreno of New Orleans said at a news conference that all passengers of the riverboat, the American Heritage, were accounted for after the crash. A city of New Orleans spokesperson added that 32 people were at local hospitals, and one person had serious injuries.

“It is a literal miracle on the Mississippi,” said Gov. Jeff Landry of Louisiana, who also spoke at the news conference.

Capt. Melanie A. Burnham, commander of Sector New Orleans for the U.S. Coast Guard, praised the work of those who rescued the ship’s passengers.

“I want to recognize the dedication, professionalism and bravery of all those first responders,” she said.

items.title: Jewish Heirs Challenge Sale of $180 Million van Gogh Painting at Sotheby’s
items.author: Catherine Hickley
items.content: <article>Heirs say “Blossoming Chestnut Trees” was sold under Nazi-era duress. The auction house says it is “committed to working toward a mutually satisfactory resolution.”</article>
items.lbText:
The heirs of the Jewish former owner of an important painting by Vincent van Gogh have asked Sotheby’s to withdraw the work from sale just days before it was to be auctioned in Manhattan, arguing that it was sold under duress in 1936 as a consequence of persecution by the Nazis.

The 1890 painting, “Châtaigniers en Fleurs (Blossoming Chestnut Trees),” carries an estimate of $180 million, the highest for any lot at this season’s art auctions, and higher than any price ever paid at auction for a work by Van Gogh. The artist painted it in Auvers-sur-Oise, near Paris, after spending two years in the south of France. The work, which is the centerpiece of the marquee fall auctions coming up next week, is backed by a financial guarantee from Sotheby’s.

The heirs, who live in the United States, say the painting was sold in Amsterdam before the Second World War as a result of financial losses sustained by their family’s publishing company under the Nazis. Gunnar Schnabel, the heirs’ Berlin lawyer, urged Sotheby’s to prove beyond a doubt that the painting was sold at market value in 1936 and that the family “would have wanted to carry out the sale even without Nazi rule.”

“Otherwise,” Schnabel wrote in a Nov. 12 email to Marco Toracca, the head of Sotheby’s restitution department, “no auction may take place.” In the email, made available to The New York Times, he said his client “is prepared to work toward a fair and just solution in the spirit of the 1998 Washington Principles,” international guidelines designed to help institutions and governments handling confiscated or Nazi-looted art.

“Blossoming Chestnut Trees” is part of the Blaquier-Arrieta collection, which Philip Hook, a former Sotheby’s executive and author, described in the auction house’s announcement of the sale as “the stuff of legend: whispered about, kept from public view.” Carlos Pedro Blaquier and Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier of Buenos Aires began collecting Impressionist and modern art in the 1960s.

items.title: Lauren Boebert Loses Re-election Bid in Colorado House Race to Eileen Laubacher
items.author: Bayliss Wagner and Kellen Browning
items.content: <article>Ms. Boebert’s loss to Eileen Laubacher in a conservative House district represents a significant victory for Democrats.</article>
items.lbText:
Representative Lauren Boebert, a hard-line Republican, on Friday narrowly lost her bid for re-election in a conservative Colorado district, according to The Associated Press , an outcome that showed just how deeply Democrats encroached into Republican territory this year.

Ms. Boebert, a fiery favorite of the MAGA movement, switched congressional districts a few years ago after her old seat in Colorado grew more competitive. But the change was not enough to keep her from being ousted by Eileen Laubacher, a Democrat and a retired rear admiral in the Navy.

Ms. Laubacher declared victory on Monday, and was leading by more than 3,000 votes when the race was called on Friday. Ms. Boebert, who amplified President Trump’s false claims of a stolen election in 2020, has not yet conceded. Her lawyer suggested last week that Ms. Boebert would request a recount.

Democrats flooded the airwaves in the district with more than $7 million worth of ads, outspending Republicans by more than 23 to 1, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact. Many of the ads fixed on Ms. Boebert’s polarizing nature and past scandals, with one calling her “uniquely unfit.” Another ad contrasted Ms. Laubacher’s profile as a Navy veteran and mother of five with headlines about Ms. Boebert.

“Lauren Boebert flips out over ‘Beetlejuice’ groping footage,’” the chyron read in one clip, referring to Ms. Boebert’s ejection from a Denver theater in 2023. Another showed Ms. Boebert cursing at the person filming.

“Like so many of us, Eileen is done with the extremists in both parties,” a narrator said in the ad, which was run by Ms. Laubacher’s campaign. “Maybe the best way to break through the noise is a little less talking and more listening.”

items.title: Inside Microsoft’s Rush to Get Back Online After a Global Outage
items.author: Karen Weise
items.content: <article>A prolonged outage left many without email and other services, the most recent reminder that the world’s technological underpinnings rely on just a few companies.</article>
items.lbText:
Late into the night Thursday, hundreds of Microsoft engineers and top executives were sitting in their darkened offices or home basements, logged into a video conference triaging a nightmare scenario for a technology company.

The world still runs on email, and much of that is processed through Microsoft Outlook. For hours, a company outage affected hospitals, schools, businesses and Congressional offices in Washington. Even Microsoft’s own staff couldn’t use email.

On the videoconference, Scott Guthrie, the senior most executive overseeing the company’s computing infrastructure, was proposing possible fixes, according to a person familiar with the call who was not authorized to speak publicly. People chewed on fingernails, rubbed their foreheads and debated how to turn off other services to prevent a “stampeding herd” so that as systems come back online, they would not be overwhelmed with new demands and shut back down.

By Friday morning, the company had apologized at least twice. It said it determined that the problem stemmed from a recent upgrade to its network, which shut down some servers, and that the systems were steadily improving. “Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage,” the company said in a statement. “While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration.”

The prolonged and widespread outage was just the most recent reminder that the technological underpinnings of modern life and business are run through just a handful of major companies. And while cyberattacks and malicious actors can target their systems, sometimes the companies learn the hard way that they can introduce devastating flaws when updating or maintaining their own global systems.

Hospitals, law enforcement and government agencies and other vital services are often left vulnerable — unable to function for hours or days at a time.

items.title: Why Jensen Huang Was Essential to Nvidia’s Rise
items.author: Tripp Mickle, Gilad Thaler, Thomas Vollkommer, Shawn Paik, Nikolay Nikolov, James Surdam, Rafaela Balster, June Kim and Mark Oltmanns
items.content: <article>Jensen Huang was the driving force at Nvidia, with 60 direct reports and no clear succession plan. Tripp Mickle, one of our technology reporters, examines Mr. Huang’s central role in the company and the artificial intelligence industry.</article>

items.title: Wall Street Loses a Powerful Dealmaker After Nvidia’s CEO Is Ousted
items.author: Maureen Farrell and Rob Copeland
items.content: <article>The ousted Nvidia chief executive was the consummate dealmaker leading the trillion-dollar A.I. build out.</article>
items.lbText:
With Jensen Huang’s abrupt ouster from Nvidia, Wall Street has lost its most powerful and profitable dealmaker.

As Mr. Huang built Nvidia from a regional chipmaker into the world’s largest company, he dispensed with the usual careful, corporate hand-wringing. He personally directed splashy deals and complicated financing structures that pumped hundreds of billions of dollars into would-be competitors, suppliers and customers.

If that made him, in the public eye, a face of the global A.I. build out, on Wall Street he represented something else: manna. His deals produced billions of dollars in fees for banks, asset managers and advisers, and Nvidia was, up until this week, spending or promising money at a speed and magnitude of little precedence.

Now Wall Street bankers, traders and even some of Nvidia’s competitors are wondering and worrying about whether Mr. Huang’s departure will slow the breakneck pace of Nvidia’s investments.

Some say that the fundamentals of Nvidia’s power are still intact, like its extreme control of the global supply of chips, the A.I. boom’s scarcest resource, the company’s deep cash coffers and the Trump administration’s warm support for the industry’s regulatory agenda. But Mr. Huang was the leader who harnessed all of those assets into a deal-making machine.

“Nvidia is the central bank of A.I.,” said Michael Edwards, director of Forum Markets, an A.I.-focused merchant bank. “Imagine the Fed without a chairman.”

items.title: Sister June Carpenter, the Oldest Shaker, Has Died
items.author: Penelope Green
items.content: <article>Now there are only two practicing members of the last active Shaker community in the United States. Sister June was 88.</article>
items.lbText:
Now there are only two practicing members of the last active Shaker community in the United States. Sister June was 88.

Sister June Carpenter in 2014. “I am the last and the least of the community,” she said, “and I’m very happy in that position.” Credit... Sean Alonzo Harris

Sister June Carpenter, a gentle librarian and one of three practicing members of the last active Shaker group in America, a Christian community of celibate pacifists, died on Nov. 3. She was 88.

Her death was announced by her community in a social media post that said she had been struggling with health and mobility issues, but did not provide further details.

At Sabbathday Lake Shaker Village in New Gloucester, Maine, there are 18 lovely brick and clapboard buildings bounded roadside by a white picket fence, set on a lake and 1,800 acres of farmland, woods and wetlands. But there aren’t legions of Shakers in residence.

At this point, there are only two: Brother Arnold Hadd, 70, and Sister April Baxter, who joined last year and is around 60.

Reports of the group’s extinction are a constant source of irritation to them. The oft-used newspaper headline, “The Last Shaker This or That,” particularly grates.

Most inquiries from the news media are politely declined because of reporters’ tendency to focus on the dwindling population. In one instance, media coverage may have exacerbated the situation. In 2006, after The Boston Globe published a story about the community headlined “The Last Man Standing,” one of its members, Brother Wayne Smith, fell in love with the reporter and left.

items.title: Book Review: ‘Promise Me, America,’ by Joe Biden
items.author: Jennifer Szalai
items.content: <article>The former president’s new memoir trumpets his achievements while justifying his decision to run for a second term and his embrace of Israel’s war in Gaza.</article>
items.lbText:
When you purchase an independently reviewed book through our site, we earn an affiliate commission.

Joe Biden wants you to know that he is proud of himself — and if his new memoir is any indication, he thinks everyone else should be proud of him, too. “Promise Me, America” begins with soaring declarations about the “long sweep of history” and the “fundamental goodness” of the United States, before turning into a minutely detailed account of his presidential accomplishments. The result reads like a mix of cover letter and campaign speech — one that’s more than 400 pages long.

It didn’t have to be this way. The post-presidential memoir is an uneven genre; to engage in sustained reflection requires some humility, a quality for which former presidents aren’t typically known. And Biden, who turns 84 on Nov. 20, can legitimately lay claim to a raft of domestic policy feats at an extraordinarily difficult time. Pandemic relief , infrastructure , clean energy , semiconductor manufacturing : He understandably wants to chronicle the hard work behind these achievements, and more.

But enumerating the wins is easy. The true test of a book like this is whether its author will own his losses, too. Biden, for his part, does not. He is so preoccupied with burnishing his legacy that he gets awkward and defensive when addressing the two issues many readers will be most curious about: his handling of the war in Gaza, and his decision to run for a second term.

From the first chapter, “History Comes Knocking,” the book runs on two tracks: steady pragmatism and accelerating grandiosity. Biden takes pains to show how, as a 78-year-old commander in chief, he assembled a “great team,” and he is plenty willing to give credit where credit is due. He makes sure to name-check his staffers, dedicating entire paragraphs to simply listing the people who traveled with him or attended a meeting. Such compilations are generous, if narratively fatal. It’s hard to sustain momentum amid a blizzard of names.

items.title: The Swingiest State Has Gone Very Red
items.author: Michael Grunwald
items.content: <article>A lot of Republicans have moved to Florida since Covid, and those newcomers really like the way Republicans are running it.</article>
items.lbText:
Credit... Damon Winter/The New York Times

Mr. Grunwald is a contributing Opinion writer. He wrote from Miami.

Democrats around the country are now asking the question weird-crime aficionados and real estate analysts have been asking for years: What is happening in Florida?

The anti-Trump stampede that trampled Republicans in blood-red bastions like Kansas, South Carolina and Texas on Nov. 3 somehow missed President Trump’s adopted state, where Republicans held on to a U.S. Senate seat, the governor’s mansion and every other statewide office. The Democratic candidate for governor, David Jolly, came just over one heartbreaking percentage point of breaking the G.O.P.’s 27-yearlock on Tallahassee.

Now the finger-pointing has begun, with Florida Democrats blaming suboptimal candidates, dubious strategies and especially the national donors who in recent years stopped investing in this former super-swing state. Florida was once the ultimate expression of America’s 50-50 politics , with eight races for governor, Senate and the presidency decided by roughly a point or less from 2000 to 2018, and frustrated Democrats believe their latest razor-thin losses prove that it can be again.

But that deep-purple Florida is gone, and it isn’t coming back anytime soon. The simple reason Democrats lost here last week is that an awful lot of Republicans have moved to Florida since the Covid pandemic, and those newcomers really like the way Republicans are running it. Gov. Ron DeSantis has remained quite popular , despite Mr. Trump’s struggles, and his vision of a “Free State of Florida” — where taxes are low, vaccines should be optional and masks are for woke losers — has become a magnet for some of the nation’s most reliable G.O.P. voters.

In 2000, when Al Gore lost the presidency to George W. Bush by a mere 537 votes in Florida, registered Democrats outnumbered Republicans here by nearly 400,000 voters, a four-point gap. But Republicans took a narrow registration lead after the pandemic in 2021, and conservative baby boomers have continued to flock here ever since. There are now 1.5 million more Republicans than Democrats, a gigantic 11-point gap, and they vote.

items.title: Jensen Huang’s Leather Jacket Isn’t Helping Him Right Now
items.author: Jacob Gallagher
items.content: <article>The Nvidia founder’s signature look branded him as a maverick. Does that image read differently now?</article>
items.lbText:
Just before Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday from Nvidia, the Silicon Valley chip juggernaut he founded three decades ago, an uncanny photo of him made the internet rounds: Huang, in what appeared to be a haute-punk Saint Laurent jacket .

It wasn’t strange to see Huang in a leather jacket. After all, rare is the public appearance where Huang doesn’t wear one. He wore one on the cover of Time in 2021 and at Nvidia’s keynote in March . In a 2016 Reddit AMA, he described himself as “the guy in the leather jacket.” (A flat descriptor that sounds as if it could be applied to a video game avatar or a cartoon character.)

But this one was well beyond his typical style: drenched in studs, with fat flapped lapels. It was also, to fashion collectors, a coveted jewel, stemming from Hedi Slimane’s tenure at the French luxury house.

Alas, it was an artifact of A.I. fakery. (Nvidia confirmed that the photo had been doctored.)

To the many gawkers who followed the chronicle of his affairs this week, the executive’s more over-the-top Billy Idol-esque leather simmered with midlife crisis energy — the clothing equivalent of a new Porsche. The studded jacket in the A.I.-generated image seemed to declare “you can’t tame me!” as his company’s stock price, and reputation, crumbled. People ate it up, even as it was debunked.

Still, the photo brought into focus how perhaps even Huang’s leather jackets — the real ones — were an indication of a man branding himself as too much of a renegade.
